concepts.title: Cultural Currents between India, Persia, Central and East Asia
concepts.definition: Between the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries a web of trade, pilgrimage and conquest carried people, books and ideas across Persia, Central Asia, East Asia and India, so art, language and belief flowed along the routes that merchants and travellers opened.
concepts.key_idea: Trade routes were culture routes: goods travelled with ideas, art and faith.
concepts.textbook_ref: hees209.txt lines 60-90 (Persia, Central Asia, East Asia links)
question_patterns: how did cultural exchange happen between India and its neighbours
which regions did India trade and share culture with in the medieval period
how did travellers spread ideas across Asia
name the routes that connected India to Persia and Central Asia
what role did merchants play in cultural exchange
give an example of an artistic influence that entered India from outside

solution_steps.explain: Land and sea routes tied India to Persia, Central Asia and East Asia.
Merchants, pilgrims, scholars and soldiers carried culture along the routes.
Languages, foods, dress, music and ideas mixed on both sides.

concepts.title: Sufi and Bhakti Currents
concepts.definition: Two devotional movements swept this age: Sufi saints of the Islamic tradition, like the Indo-Persian Sufi poet Amir Khusrau who blended Indian and Persian song, and the Bhakti saints who preached loving devotion in local tongues, both carrying religion to the common people.
concepts.key_idea: Sufi and Bhakti saints took faith out of the clergy's hands and into people's languages.
concepts.textbook_ref: hees209.txt lines 330-420 (continuation and evolution, Amir Khusrau, Indian Persian and Arabic singing)
question_patterns: who was Amir Khusrau and why is he remembered
what are the main teachings of the Sufi saints
how did the Bhakti movement reach ordinary people
compare the Bhakti and Sufi movements
how did Indian, Persian and Arabic singing traditions blend
why did saints compose in local languages

solution_steps.explain: Sufi khanqahs and Bhakti gatherings drew crowds beyond temples and mosques.
Poetry and song in Hindavi and regional tongues replaced distant classical forms.
Khusrau's music wove Indian and Persian strands into a shared culture.

concepts.title: Variations in Role and Status: Women and Social Groups
concepts.definition: Status in medieval society varied by region, caste and gender: women's roles ranged from royal regents and poet-saints to weavers working in household workshops, and social groups rose or fell as new professions and sects opened different paths.
concepts.key_idea: Medieval society was layered and mobile - gender, caste and occupation shaped each life differently.
concepts.textbook_ref: hees209.txt lines 520-540 (variations in their role and status)
question_patterns: how did the status of women vary in medieval society
name women saints or rulers of this period
how did new professions change the social order
compare the lives of artisans and nobles in the period
why did social status differ from region to region
give examples of social mobility in medieval India

solution_steps.explain: Customs differed by kingdom, caste and community.
Saints, queens and traders show women and lower groups shaping public life.
New sects and professions offered routes around old hierarchies.

concepts.title: Education and Knowledge Traditions
concepts.definition: Learning flourished in maktabs, madrasas, pathshalas and temple schools: mathematics, astronomy, medicine, music and craft knowledge were taught and exchanged, with manuscripts moving across Asia to keep India part of the medieval world of learning.
concepts.key_idea: Schools of many faiths and craft guilds of many skills kept knowledge alive and travelling.
question_patterns: where did students study in medieval India
what subjects were taught in madrasas and pathshalas
how did knowledge travel between India and other lands
name the centres of learning of the medieval period
what role did manuscripts play in education
compare the education of this period with today's schooling

solution_steps.explain: Maktabs, madrasas, pathshalas and temple centres taught different communities.
Religion, language, mathematics, astronomy and medicine shared the syllabus.
Copied manuscripts and travelling scholars moved learning across borders.
